title: To font-size, or not to font-size
excerpt: Article exploring different approaches to responsive typography in CSS, comparing viewport units, calc(), and traditional responsive breakpoints.
content:
By Mads Stoumann

When creating responsive web sites, there are multiple strategies for font-sizing.

At the agency I work at (Valtech), we typically use responsive breakpoints for changing font-sizes. With responsive breakpoints, we might change the root font-size (on which other sizes are based, using em), like this:

@media (min-width: 640px)  { html { font-size: 13px; } }
@media (min-width: 768px)  { html { font-size: 14px; } }
@media (min-width: 1024px) { html { font-size: 15px; } }
@media (min-width: 1280px) { html { font-size: 16px; } }
@media (min-width: 1600px) { html { font-size: 17px; } }

Since everything is based on the root font-size (using em), elements will scale nicely, when the media-queries kick in.

Another approach is using viewport units:

html { font-size: 2.5vw; }

By using viewport units for font-sizing, the text itself becomes responsive, and will grow along with the viewport width. It’s an interesting technique!

However, by purely using viewport units, at small viewport widths, the fonts will become too small to read. And on large viewport widths, they’ll become too big!

You can use media-queries for setting min/max font-sizes, but you can also use calc(), a CSS-function for calculating dimensions. Read this excellent article for inspiration!

I’ve played a bit with calc() myself, you can see the result on Codepen:
http://codepen.io/stoumann/pen/QEqaXv

The essential parts are:

$min-font-size: 13px;
$max-font-size: 17px;
$min-screen: 320px;
$max-screen: 1600px;

html {
  font-size: calc(#{$min-font-size} + (#{$max-font-size} - #{$min-font-size}) * (100vw - #{$min-screen}) / (#{$max-screen} - #{$min-screen}));
}

@media (max-width: $min-screen) {
  html { font-size: $min-font-size; }
}
@media (min-width: $max-screen) {
  html { font-size: $max-font-size; }
}

The only downside of the calc()-technique is using px-values, instead of ems.

Below is the full Codepen. I’ve used SASS and split the lines, so it’s easier to read.
Toggle between “Use breakpoints” and “Use calc” to see the difference.

See the Pen Font-size: breakpoints or calc? by Mads Stoumann (@stoumann) on CodePen.

Happy coding!

title: You spin me round (like a record)
excerpt: CSS animation tutorial creating a spinning vinyl record effect using keyframe animations and CSS transforms.
content:
By Mads Stoumann

I have a large collection of vinyl records, and music is an important part of my life. Hence my experiment today, which is to (re-) create a spinning vinyl record using only CSS.

I’ve created various effects in the past, using Flash, canvas and SVG — but I wanted to see what could be accomplished with just CSS. And it looks pretty neat!

I can’t really see a use-case for it, except a (very different!) icon for a music-player.

Hope you like it.

Happy coding!

title: SVG, pair of dice
excerpt: Tutorial on creating interactive SVG dice with JavaScript-controlled animations and pseudo-3D effects using CSS gradients.
content:
By Mads Stoumann

Last week I got my hands on a simple dice game: Yatzy.

I like to play around with SVG and animations, so I thought I’d create a digital version of the game using CSS (SCSS) for the pseudo-3D-look of the dice, and JavaScript for controlling the throw.

In this version, clicking on a die will “lock” it, so that the next throw won’t change that die. The locked die will have a red shadow.

Clicking “Roll” will throw all unlocked dice.

By the way, I’ve used an old-school random-snippet (I thought I’d share it!):

function getRandom(nMin, nMax) {
  return ~~(Math.random() * (nMax - nMin + 1)) + nMin;
}

Enjoy!

Happy coding!

title: Front-End Detective
excerpt: Sometimes stuff breaks. On the web, something that was working perfectly yesterday, might suddenly not work today.
content:
Sometimes stuff breaks. On the web, something that was working perfectly yesterday, might suddenly not work today. "Why?" — might a client ask — "do we have to pay for fixing something we already paid for."

I can understand this frustration, and want to illustrate why it is so, by conveying two recent cases, I had to debug and solve.

Case number 1

A while ago, I created a Pen on Codepen with responsive SVG's:

As usual, I tested in all evergreen browsers, and it looked good.
Then, to my horror, a couple of weeks ago, I opened the Pen in Safari.
Only one of the SVG's were displayed, the rest — vanished!

It took a while to figure out that Safari 9.0.3+ has a bug rendering SVG's if you're using a drop-shadow filter. It will, hopefully, soon be fixed.

If you're reading this post on Safari 9.0.3+ you'll see only one SVG as well.
If you want to see the rest, click on the SCSS-tab and delete this line:

@include prefixed(filter, drop-shadow($shadow));

Case number 2

The second case were much harder to debug. A couple of days before a big presentation, I wanted to double-check all the pages, I was going to demo.
To my horror, several pages crashed Safari.

Yes.
Crashed!

By investigating and comparing, I found out, that all the pages that were crashing, were using a technique known as SVG Sprites:

<svg><use xlink:href="svg/social.svg#icon-apple"></use></svg>

However, after further debugging, I could conclude that the crashing was a combination of the CSS on the page and the SVG sprites.

Slowly, by trying out all the versions of the stylesheet for the pages I had, I found a two-week old version that didn't crash Safari! By comparing this with the current version, commenting potential lines out, I finally ended up with the culprit:

::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb:window-inactive {
  background: #fefefe;
}

It doesn't make any sense at all, does it? How can the styling of a scrollbar crash Safari on pages with SVG <use> – and not only that, the affected pages don't even use the scrollbar.

But it can — and to prove it, I've created a "crash page", you can try out in Safari on either your Mac, iPhone or iPad (version 9.0.3+).

Crash Safari here!

Here's the simple code behind:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en" class="blocks">
<head>
	<title>Crash Safari</title>
	<meta charset="UTF-8">
	<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, maximum-scale=1, shrink-to-fit=no">
	<style>
	::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb:window-inactive {
     	background: #fefefe; 
	}
	</style>
</head>
<body>
	<a href="#apple" itemprop="url" title="Apple">
		<svg><use xlink:href="svg/social.svg#icon-apple"></use></svg>
	</a>
</body>
</html>

So — in conclusion — things that worked perfectly yesterday, might not work tomorrow, and that's (also) a part of the life of a front-end developer to debug and figure out!

Happy coding.

title: Thinking in modules
excerpt: The author discusses challenges with inheriting code from other developers and proposes a modular approach to sharing frontend code.
content:
By Mads Stoumann

I think, inheriting code from other developers, can be a struggle. There, I said it!
That's because not two developers think alike — everyone has his or hers way of doing things.

Having said that, here's my personal take on how to tackle code-share between (front-end-) developers:

Think in modules.

No matter what you create on a site, being it an article, an accordion-, spot- or a video-block, think of it as an individual module, with it's own version number and "module-like" structure.

Happy coding!

content:

A while ago, I wrote a blog-post called The Curse Of The Click-Delay, on how to avoid the 300 ms click-delay on touch-devices, using a small JavaScript.

Since then, iOS has been updated with a new CSS-property:

— and that property, along with some other settings, removes the delay without using JavaScript!
